comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams track and manage their work. This comparison is useful for teams currently using Jira who are considering switching to a self-hosted, free alternative. The core use case for both tools is issue tracking and project management, and the key reason someone would switch is to reduce costs and gain more control over their data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira is a paid tool with a per-user monthly fee, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: With Plane, teams have full control over their data, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Jira is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Jira is designed to scale with large teams, while Plane's scalability depends on the team's self-hosting capabilities.
* Integration with Git: Jira has native integration with Git, while Plane relies on third-party integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira Pros:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Native integration with Git
* Scalable with large teams
* Robust feature set
* Good customer support
**Jira Cons:**
* Expensive, especially for large teams
* Limited control over data
* Proprietary license
* Limited customization options
**Plane Pros:**
* Free and self-hosted
* Full control over data
* Customizable and extensible
* Apache 2.0 license
* Cost-effective
**Plane Cons:**
* Requires technical expertise to set up and maintain
* Limited native integrations
* Scalability depends on self-hosting capabilities
* Limited customer support
* Still in development, with some features missing

## When to Choose Each
Jira is a good choice for large teams that need a scalable, easy-to-use project management tool with native integration with Git. It's also a good choice for teams that don't mind paying a premium for a proprietary tool with good customer support. Plane, on the other hand, is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that want a free, self-hosted alternative with full control over their data. It's also a good choice for teams with technical expertise that can handle the setup and maintenance of a self-hosted tool.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a Plane instance on your own server.
3. Use the Plane import tool to import your Jira data.
4. Configure Plane to match your team's workflow and needs.
5. Test and verify that all data has been imported correctly.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it's still in development and lacks some key features. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane's scalability depends on the team's self-hosting capabilities, which can be a challenge for large teams. However, for small to medium-sized teams with technical expertise, Plane is a great alternative to Jira, offering a free, self-hosted solution with full control over data.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need native Git integration
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that want to reduce costs
* Teams with technical expertise that can handle self-hosting and maintenance
* Teams that prioritize data ownership and control
* Teams that don't need advanced features like agile project planning

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted. You only need to pay for the server costs.
### Can I migrate my Jira data to Plane?
Yes, you can export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format and import it into Plane using the Plane import tool.
### Is Plane scalable?
Plane's scalability depends on the team's self-hosting capabilities. It may not be suitable for very large teams.
### Does Plane have native Git integration?
No, Plane relies on third-party integrations for Git.
### Is Plane production-ready?
Not yet, as it's still in development and lacks some key features.

title: Trello vs WeKan

# Trello vs WeKan (2026)

## Overview
Trello and WeKan are project management tools that help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering switching from Trello to WeKan, particularly those concerned about data ownership and self-hosting options. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration and task management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Trello offers a free plan with limited features, while WeKan is free and open-source, allowing for self-hosting.
* Data Ownership: WeKan allows teams to host their data on their own servers, giving them full control and ownership, whereas Trello stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup Complexity: WeKan requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, especially for self-hosting, whereas Trello is easy to set up and use.
* Scalability: Trello is designed to scale with large teams and enterprises, while WeKan's scalability depends on the team's ability to manage their own server infrastructure.
* Integration: Trello has a wider range of integrations with third-party tools and services, including Google Drive and Slack, whereas WeKan has limited integrations but allows for custom development.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $250/month (standard plan) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1000/month (standard plan) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Trello:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Scalable and reliable infrastructure
* Mobile apps for on-the-go access
* Limited control over data ownership and storage
**WeKan:**
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Customizable and extensible
* Community-driven development
* Limited integrations with third-party tools
* Requires technical expertise for setup and maintenance

## When to Choose Each
Trello is suitable for teams that prioritize ease of use, scalability, and a wide range of integrations. It's ideal for large teams and enterprises that need a reliable and feature-rich project management tool. WeKan, on the other hand, is perfect for teams that value data ownership, customization, and control over their infrastructure. It's suitable for small to medium-sized teams with technical expertise and a desire for self-hosting.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Trello boards in JSON format using the Trello API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a WeKan instance on your own server or use a hosted solution.
3. Use the WeKan import tool to migrate your Trello data, including boards, lists, and cards.
4. Configure your WeKan instance to match your Trello setup, including custom fields and integrations.
5. Test your WeKan instance to ensure a smooth transition and resolve any issues that arise.

## Our Take
WeKan is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise and has limited integrations with third-party tools. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that WeKan's scalability depends on the team's ability to manage their own server infrastructure. However, for teams that value data ownership and customization, WeKan is a viable alternative to Trello, and we recommend it for small to medium-sized teams with technical expertise.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need extensive integrations with third-party tools
* Teams with technical expertise that want to self-host their project management tool
* Organizations that prioritize data ownership and control over their infrastructure
* Teams that require customization and extensibility in their project management tool
* Businesses that want to avoid per-user costs and prefer a free, open-source solution

## FAQ
### Is WeKan free?
Yes, WeKan is free and open-source, allowing for self-hosting and customization.
### Can I migrate my Trello data to WeKan?
Yes, you can export your Trello data in JSON format and import it into WeKan using the WeKan import tool.
### Does WeKan have mobile apps?
No, WeKan does not have official mobile apps, but it can be accessed through a web browser on mobile devices.
### Is WeKan scalable?
WeKan's scalability depends on the team's ability to manage their own server infrastructure, which can be a limitation for large teams.
### Can I integrate WeKan with Google Drive?
Not yet, but WeKan allows for custom development and integrations, so it's possible to create a custom integration with Google Drive.

title: Dropbox vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Dropbox vs Nextcloud

## Overview

Dropbox is one of the original cloud storage services offering simple file sync. Nextcloud is the most popular self-hosted cloud platform combining file storage, calendar, contacts, video calls, and 400+ apps.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Dropbox charges $9.99-$16.58/user/month; Nextcloud is free to self-host
- **Storage**: Nextcloud storage is limited only by your server disk space
- **Feature breadth**: Nextcloud is far more than storage; it is a full Google Workspace alternative
- **Privacy**: Nextcloud on your own server means only you can access your data
- **Setup**: Dropbox is instant; Nextcloud requires Docker setup

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Dropbox | Nextcloud |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $9.99-$16.58/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$500/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,998/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Dropbox

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Nextcloud

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [nextcloud/server](https://github.com/nextcloud/server) * ~27k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Dropbox if:** Dropbox suits individuals or small teams wanting simple reliable file sync with no infrastructure to manage.

**Choose Nextcloud if:** Nextcloud suits privacy-focused organizations wanting to eliminate cloud subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Download all Dropbox files locally, then upload to Nextcloud via the web interface or desktop sync client.

## Our Take

Nextcloud is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Dropbox tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Nextcloud instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Dropbox, switching to self-hosted Nextcloud will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Dropbox until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Dropbox paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Nextcloud free to use?
Yes. Nextcloud is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Dropbox to Nextcloud?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Dropbox data, follow the Nextcloud import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Nextcloud get regular updates?
Yes. Nextcloud has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Nextcloud without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Nextcloud development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Dropbox](https://dropbox.com) and [Nextcloud](https://nextcloud.com) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Nextcloud is a free, self-hosted alternative to Dropbox. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

Google Workspace and Nextcloud are two popular productivity and collaboration platforms that cater to the needs of individuals, teams, and organizations. * Cost: Google Workspace charges $6-$18 per user per month, while Nextcloud is free and open-source, with costs limited to server maintenance.

* Setup complexity: Google Workspace is generally easier to set up and requires less technical expertise, while Nextcloud requires more technical knowledge to self-host.
* Scalability: Google Workspace is highly scalable and can handle large teams and organizations, while Nextcloud's scalability depends on the server infrastructure.
* Integration: Google Workspace has native integration with Google Drive, while Nextcloud has integration with various third-party apps through its marketplace.

| Aspect | Google Workspace | Nextcloud |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $6-$18/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |

**Google Workspace:**
